hints: Focus on the oxidation number of nitrogen in each ion and product, since nitrogen is the only element that changes.
In $\text{NH}_4^+$ nitrogen is -3 and in $\text{NO}_3^-$ nitrogen is +5, while in $\text{N}_2\text{O}$ nitrogen is +1, so work out who is oxidised and who is reduced.
Remember disproportionation needs one oxidation state splitting into two different states, so check if that matches two different states joining into one here.
walkthrough:
**Write the equation and assign oxidation numbers**

Start by writing the balanced equation and tracking nitrogen, as H and O do not change.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3 \rightarrow \text{N}_2\text{O} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Find nitrogen in the reactants**

In $\text{NH}_4^+$, H is +1, so N is -3. In $\text{NO}_3^-$, O is -2, so N is +5. These are two very different starting points.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{N in NH}_4^+ = -3, \quad \text{N in NO}_3^- = +5$$

**Find nitrogen in the products and decide redox**

In $\text{N}_2\text{O}$, O is -2, so each N is +1. One N goes from -3 to +1, that is oxidation, so $\text{NH}_4^+$ is the reducing agent. The other N goes from +5 to +1, that is reduction, so $\text{NO}_3^-$ is the oxidising agent. Oxidation and reduction both occur, so it is redox.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{N in N}_2\text{O} = +1$$

**Test for disproportionation**

Disproportionation means the same element in the same oxidation state is both oxidised and reduced at the same time. Here two different oxidation states, -3 and +5, both become +1. That is the opposite, comproportionation, so statement 4 is false. Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct.

options.A: Includes statements 1, 2 and 3 which are correct, but wrongly includes 4. This is the trap of calling any reaction with one element ending in one product a disproportionation, when here two different initial states converge, which is comproportionation.
options.B: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. N(-3) in ammonium is oxidised to N(+1), so it reduces the nitrate and acts as a reducing agent. N(+5) in nitrate is reduced to N(+1), so it oxidises the ammonium and acts as an oxidising agent. The reaction is therefore redox but not disproportionation.
options.C: Correct to include 3 and to recognise redox, but wrong on two counts. It misses that 1 and 2 are also true, and it wrongly accepts 4. Disproportionation requires one oxidation state to split into a higher and a lower state.
options.D: Correct that it is a redox reaction, but incomplete. Students choosing this often spot the change in oxidation number but do not link oxidation to reducing agent behaviour and reduction to oxidising agent behaviour for statements 1 and 2.
